beats.narration_text: Kimi K3 costs a fraction of frontier models. And Moonshot says it passed its safety evaluations. Are both claims true? The cost story is real and durable — it doesn't depend on benchmark setup. The safety story needs two reads: Moonshot's version, and the independent UK/US government assessment. Here's both.
Act One: Cheap.

props.heading: Fig. 13: Cost vs. Quality
props.body: K3's API pricing sits dramatically below frontier proprietary models for comparable independent-eval performance.

beats.narration_text: Figure 13: cost versus quality scatter. K3's API pricing sits dramatically below frontier proprietary models for comparable independent-eval performance.

graphic.description: Scatter plot. X-axis: price per million tokens (log scale). Y-axis: independent eval score (0–100). K3 labeled in gold in the lower-right quadrant — low cost, high performance. Competitors labeled in upper-right quadrant — high cost, similar performance. Axes clean. Colors: gold #e0b341, blue #6fb0d6, terracotta #d9704e.

beats.narration_text: This claim is the most durable result in the paper. It doesn't depend on harness choice or benchmark modification. Token prices are public. You can verify them yourself.

For practitioners running agentic workloads at scale, this is the number that matters. If K3 performs at a top-tier level — and the independent evals support that — and costs a fraction of that, the economic calculus shifts.

props.heading: One Honest Limit
props.body: Self-hosted 2.8T on your own H100s is a very different bill than the API price. Fig. 13 is API versus API. It says nothing about on-premise total cost of ownership.

beats.narration_text: One honest limit: self-hosted 2.8 trillion parameters on your own H100s is a very different bill than the API price. Figure 13 is API versus API. It says nothing about on-premise total cost of ownership.
Act Two: The Cyber Section.

props.heading: Section 6.2.2: Cybersecurity
props.body: Moonshot ran K3 through a safety evaluation and framed the result as a 'lower bound' — the model has limited offensive cyber capability. 'Lower bound' is honest language. They're setting a floor, not a ceiling.

beats.narration_text: Section 6.2.2: Cybersecurity. Moonshot ran K3 through a safety evaluation and framed the result as a 'lower bound' — the model has limited offensive cyber capability. 'Lower bound' is honest language. They're setting a floor, not a ceiling.

But 'lower bound' is also careful language. It leaves room for the full capability to be higher than tested. What it didn't anticipate was that the independent government evaluators would be much more direct.
Act Three: What AISI and CAISI found.

graphic.description: Map card. UK and US flagged positions connected to a joint report label in the center. Label reads 'UK AISI + US CAISI — Joint Cyber Capability Evaluation'. Background: dark navy #2E3440. Accent: terracotta #D97757. Clean, no decorative detail.

beats.narration_text: UK AISI and US CAISI — the AI safety institutes operating under the Bletchley and Seoul AI governance agreements — ran K3 through a joint cyber capability evaluation. Independent. No Moonshot involvement.

props.heading: AISI/CAISI Results
props.body: 0 of 41 arbitrary-code-execution tasks completed. 32% overall score on the full cyber task battery. That's the number that went into the official joint assessment.

beats.narration_text: Results: zero of 41 arbitrary-code-execution tasks completed. 32% overall score on the full cyber task battery. That's the number that went into the official joint assessment.

graphic.description: Bar chart. Two bars side by side. K3 bar: 32%, gold #e0b341. US frontier average bar: 76%, steel blue #6fb0d6. Gap between them labeled '2.4× below US models'. Y-axis 0–100%. Title: 'Cyber Task Battery Score'. Clean, EB Garamond labels.

beats.narration_text: Context: US frontier models average 76% on the same battery. K3 at 32% is not a close second. It's less than half the frontier capability score.
Credit where it's due: Moonshot published this result. They included the AISI and CAISI assessment in their own tech report. Most labs don't disclose unfavorable third-party evals. This one did.

graphic.description: Number line from 0% to 100%. Gold marker at 32% labeled 'K3 — lower bound (AISI result)'. Grey marker at 76% labeled 'US frontier avg'. Arrow from 32% to 76% labeled '+44 pts'. Annotation below: 'Lower bound: floor, not ceiling — but the floor is low in absolute terms.' Colors: gold #e0b341, grey #888.

beats.narration_text: 'Lower bound' framing revisited: Moonshot knew the external evaluators would find limited capability and said so preemptively. The transparency is real. The optimism in the original framing — leading with 'lower bound' as if it's modest — was overplayed once you see 32% versus 76%.
Act Four: What the numbers mean.

props.heading: 32% ≠ Safe
props.body: 32% on arbitrary-code-execution does not mean safe. It means the model cannot autonomously mount most attacks on that evaluation set. That's one threat model. Scaffolded attacks, human-guided use, jailbreaks — different threat models.

beats.narration_text: 32% on arbitrary-code-execution does not mean safe. It means the model cannot autonomously mount most attacks on that evaluation set. That's one threat model. Scaffolded attacks, human-guided use, jailbreaks — those are different threat models.

graphic.description: Three-tier vertical taxonomy diagram. Mode 1: 'Autonomous — model executes attack unassisted' — labeled 'TESTED' in gold. Mode 2: 'Scaffolded — human harness improves model attack capability' — labeled 'NOT IN SCOPE' in grey. Mode 3: 'Human-directed — model as component, human provides judgment' — labeled 'NOT IN SCOPE' in grey. Clean EB Garamond. Background: dark. Colors: #e0b341, #888888.

beats.narration_text: Three threat modes. Autonomous: model executes attack unassisted. Scaffolded: human builds a harness that improves the model's attack capability. Human-directed: model as a component, human provides judgment. The AISI test covers only mode one.
And the 76% US frontier number raises its own question — what are we building toward? A 76% arbitrary-code-execution score is not a safety benchmark to aspire to. It's a risk signal.
Act Five: What they admitted.

props.heading: CritPt: 23.4 — Lowest in the Table
props.body: Critical thinking and deductive reasoning — 23.4. The lowest score K3 has on the entire 34-benchmark table. Fable 5: 28.6. GPT-5.6 Sol: 32.3. GPT-5.5: 27.1.

beats.narration_text: One more honest disclosure: CritPt — critical thinking and deductive reasoning — 23.4. The lowest score K3 has on the entire 34-benchmark table. Clearly trailing: Fable 5 at 28.6, GPT-5.6 Sol at 32.3, GPT-5.5 at 27.1.

graphic.description: Bar chart. Six models, all showing CritPt scores. K3 bar: 23.4, gold #e0b341, clearly the shortest — gap to next-lowest labeled. Other models range 27–32. Y-axis 0–35. Title: 'CritPt Score — Critical Thinking & Deductive Reasoning'. Labels: K3, Fable 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.5 + two others as placeholders. EB Garamond. Clean dark background.

beats.narration_text: Far enough below the field that it's probably not sampling noise. This is a real gap in research-level reasoning, acknowledged in the same paper that leads with K3 near the top of most everything else.

The combination — limited cyber capability, lowest critical-thinking score — actually reads coherently. A model built and trained for long-horizon coding and tool orchestration, not adversarial deductive reasoning.

props.heading: Disclosure Pattern
props.body: The pattern of what they disclosed versus what they could have hidden is better than average for an industry tech report. That's a calibration input. Not a correctness certificate.

beats.narration_text: The pattern of what they disclosed versus what they could have hidden is better than average for an industry tech report. That's a calibration input. Not a correctness certificate.

props.verdict: The cost claim is the most durable result here — independently verifiable, harness-independent, and practically significant for practitioners. The cyber story requires two reads: the carefully-hedged Moonshot version and the blunter AISI/CAISI one. Weight the independent assessors. The disclosed weaknesses — 0 of 41 ACE tasks completed, CritPt at the bottom of the table — are real signals about what this model is built for. Give Moonshot credit for publishing them.

Cheap — and the Cyber Question.

Verdict. The cost story is real — K3 runs at roughly twenty times less cost than frontier models, holding regardless of benchmark setup. The safety story is different. Moonshot's own evaluation found thirty-two percent on cyber tasks — a lower bound they declared themselves. Independent government assessors found zero autonomously completed attacks out of forty-one. K3 does not meaningfully lower the bar for autonomous cyber attacks. Scaffolded and scripted modes: limited uplift found. Not zero — limited. Trust the cost claim. Treat the safety claim as provisional.
